Name: Achernar
Note: Marks the southern end of the river Eridanus.

Name: Acrux
Note: Brightest star in the Southern Cross, at the foot of the cross.

Name: Aldebaran
Note: Marks the eye of the bull; not physically in the Hyades cluster it appears in front of.

Name: Altair
Note: One of the three stars of the Summer Triangle.

Name: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)
Note: Nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way; faint naked-eye smudge in Andromeda.

Name: Antares
Note: Red supergiant whose name means 'rival of Mars'.

Name: Arcturus
Note: Brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere.

Name: Betelgeuse
Note: Red supergiant marking Orion's shoulder.

Name: Canopus
Note: Second-brightest star in the night sky.

Name: Capella
Note: Actually a pair of close binary star pairs.

Name: Castor
Note: The fainter of Gemini's twin stars despite being labeled Alpha; actually a system of six stars.

Name: Cat's Eye Nebula (NGC 6543)
Note: One of the first planetary nebulae studied spectroscopically; a dying Sun-like star's glowing ejected shell, in Draco.

Name: Crab Nebula (M1)
Note: Supernova remnant in Taurus from a star seen exploding in 1054 CE; the first object in Messier's catalogue.

Name: Deneb
Note: One of the most luminous stars known; forms the Summer Triangle with Vega and Altair.

Name: Eagle Nebula (M16)
Note: Star-forming region in Serpens; its central dust columns are the 'Pillars of Creation' imaged by Hubble.

Name: Fomalhaut
Note: Name means 'mouth of the fish'.

Name: Gacrux
Note: Red giant at the top of the Southern Cross; one of the nearest red giants to the Sun.

Name: Hadar
Note: Beta Centauri; with Rigil Kentaurus, one of the two Pointers that lead to the Southern Cross.

Name: Helix Nebula (NGC 7293)
Note: One of the closest planetary nebulae to Earth, in Aquarius; nicknamed the 'Eye of God'.

Name: Hubble Deep Field
Note: A tiny, seemingly empty patch of sky in Ursa Major that a 1995 Hubble exposure revealed to contain thousands of distant galaxies.

Name: Jewel Box (NGC 4755)
Note: Bright, colourful young open cluster beside Beta Crucis in the Southern Cross.

Name: Large Magellanic Cloud
Note: Milky Way satellite galaxy, visible naked-eye from the southern hemisphere, in Dorado/Mensa.

Name: Mimosa
Note: Second-brightest star of the Southern Cross, at the eastern end of its crossbar.

Name: North Celestial Pole
Note: Marked closely (but not exactly) by Polaris, in Ursa Minor.

Name: Omega Centauri
Note: The brightest and most massive globular cluster in the Milky Way, visible naked-eye in Centaurus.

Name: Orion Nebula (M42)
Note: Star-forming nebula visible to the naked eye in Orion's Sword.

Name: Pleiades (M45)
Note: Bright open star cluster in Taurus, the 'Seven Sisters'.

Name: Pollux
Note: Brighter of the two Gemini twin stars (with Castor).

Name: Procyon
Note: Name means 'before the dog', rising just before Sirius.

Name: Regulus
Note: Marks the heart of the lion; sits almost exactly on the ecliptic.

Name: Rigel
Note: Blue supergiant marking Orion's foot.

Name: Rigil Kentaurus (Alpha Centauri)
Note: Closest star system to the Sun.

Name: Sirius
Note: Brightest star in the night sky.

Name: Small Magellanic Cloud
Note: Milky Way satellite galaxy, visible naked-eye from the southern hemisphere, in Tucana.

Name: South Celestial Pole
Note: No bright star marks it; nearest naked-eye star is faint Sigma Octantis.

Name: Spica
Note: Brightest star in Virgo.

Name: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)
Note: Third-largest galaxy in the Local Group; a naked-eye challenge object under dark skies.

Name: VY Canis Majoris
Note: Red hypergiant in Canis Major, one of the largest known stars.

Name: Vega
Note: Was the northern pole star ~12,000 BCE.
